concepts.name: Real estate and credit cycles
concepts.origin: Quality bar 6.1
concepts.mechanism: Space markets clear slowly. Developers build on today's rents, and new supply arrives two or three years later, often after demand has turned. Vacancy then rises while rents and values fall together. Credit is easiest near the peak, when values are highest and recent losses are lowest. So loans made near a peak are sized on the top of the curve and default more often (MIT lec. 12: lifetime default by origination year tracks the cycle). A lender that sizes on current value is betting that value at maturity will be similar. The cycle explains why that bet fails in clusters, not one loan at a time.

concepts.name: Lender types, funding routes and the capital partner's credit box
concepts.origin: Syllabi B2 (CMBS and securitization; REIT debt; loan valuation context)
concepts.mechanism: Most non-bank business-purpose lenders do not hold their loans. They fund through a warehouse line, a whole-loan sale or a securitization. Each capital partner has its own eligibility rules, advance rates and repurchase rights. A loan outside those rules cannot be financed or sold at par. So the partner's box quietly sets the lender's credit box. Bank and REIT lenders face different regulators and capital rules, which explains why they price and size differently.

concepts.name: The regulatory perimeter: business-purpose versus consumer credit
concepts.origin: Added so C1 has a home concept (quality bar 6.2)
concepts.mechanism: Consumer credit law assumes a household borrower who cannot easily judge loan terms. Business-purpose and entity loans fall outside most of it. That exemption lowers cost and speeds closing. It also creates a strong incentive to dress a consumer loan as a business loan. If the purpose test fails, the lender can lose the exemption and face consumer-law remedies on a loan priced as commercial [VERIFY: 12 CFR 1026.3(a); checked 18 Nov 2026 per Course Bible §1]. Fair-lending law is the exception: it follows the credit, not only the consumer.

concepts.name: Default as the borrower's option to walk away
concepts.origin: Quality bar 6.1
concepts.mechanism: A non-recourse borrower can hand back the property instead of paying. That is a put option on the property, with the loan balance as the strike. The option gains value as property value falls toward the balance, and as value becomes more volatile. Equity below the loan is what keeps the option out of the money. That is the economic reason for LTV limits, equity-first rules and lower leverage on riskier collateral. Recourse and springing carve-outs raise the cost of exercising the option, so they change behavior, not only recovery.

misconceptions.correction: A borrower with cash may still stop paying when the property is worth less than the loan. Model convention: that figure assumes no amortization and a value drift of about 1.4% a year (log), measured at maturity only. At zero drift it is about 1 in 4 (23.4%). concepts.name: Agency problems: adverse selection, moral hazard, originate-to-distribute and sponsor incentives
concepts.origin: Quality bar 6.1
concepts.mechanism: Borrowers know more about their projects than lenders do. Raising the rate to cover unknown risk drives away safe borrowers first (adverse selection, credit rationing). After closing, a borrower with little equity left gains from riskier choices, or from "bleeding" the property (moral hazard). A lender that sells its loans keeps less of the loss, so its screening incentive weakens (originate-to-distribute). Risk retention [VERIFY: 17 CFR 246.4(a); checked 22 Nov 2026 per needs analysis §4] and repurchase rights push that loss back. Sponsors paid by promote share the upside but not the downside below their equity. Collateral, equity first, guaranties and covenants are the lender's answers to all four.

concepts.name: Concentration risk
concepts.origin: Quality bar 6.1
concepts.mechanism: Loans to one sponsor, one state or one property type tend to fail together. Diversification only works if defaults are not correlated. A sponsor cap limits single-name exposure: one sponsor's failure can hit several loans at once. Portfolio buckets limit correlated exposure to one market or product. Capital partners and bank buyers set their own limits for the same reason.

concepts.name: Risk ratings and credit migration
concepts.origin: Added: core lender concept (needs analysis S4, K4)
concepts.mechanism: A risk rating is the lender's shorthand for default likelihood and loss if default happens. Ratings migrate before losses appear. Catching a move from pass to special mention buys time to act while options remain. Ratings also drive reporting, accrual status and the allowance, so a late downgrade understates risk to managers and capital partners.

concepts.name: Time value of money and mortgage mathematics
concepts.origin: Syllabi B2 (four rules)
concepts.mechanism: A loan is a set of dated cash flows. Present value turns them into one comparable number. Four rules run every schedule. Interest is the prior balance times the period rate. Principal is the payment less interest. The new balance is the old balance less principal, and the first balance is the loan. Each loan type fixes one column and lets the others follow. Lenders need this to know the balance at maturity, which is what the exit must repay.

concepts.name: Loan types and amortization
concepts.origin: Syllabi B2
concepts.mechanism: Interest-only loans keep the payment low and leave the whole balance for the exit. Amortizing loans repay principal and lower the balance the exit must cover. Partial interest-only sits between the two. The choice shifts risk between today's cash flow test and tomorrow's refinance test. Constant-amortization, graduated-payment and negative-amortization loans are rare in business-purpose lending; they are named so the learner can spot them.

concepts.name: Contract rate, yield to maturity and expected return
concepts.origin: Syllabi B2
concepts.mechanism: The note rate is what the contract says. Points and fees paid up front raise the lender's yield, and more so if the loan pays off early. Default lowers the return actually earned below the promised yield. A lender that compares loans on note rate alone misprices short loans with points and risky loans with high coupons. C3 teaches contract rate versus yield; C8 adds expected return through expected loss (TM-19).

concepts.name: Interest-rate risk on floating-rate loans
concepts.origin: Quality bar 6.1 (interest-rate risk, split from refinance and extension risk)
concepts.mechanism: A floating loan moves rate risk to the borrower. When SOFR rises, the payment rises while the property's income does not. Rate risk the lender passed on comes back as credit risk if coverage falls below 1.00x. A rate cap limits the borrower's rate, so the lender sizes and tests coverage at the cap strike, not at today's rate. When a cap expires, replacing it at higher cost is a second shock.

concepts.name: Pro forma realism and submarket evidence
concepts.origin: Syllabi B2
concepts.mechanism: Sellers and brokers forecast the best plausible case. A lender repaid from cash flow must underwrite the likely case. Rent growth, vacancy, capital spending and exit cap rate are the usual places where a pro forma hides optimism. Testing each against submarket evidence turns a sales document into an underwriting input.

concepts.name: Cash-flow coverage and break-even
concepts.origin: Added so C4 has a cash-flow mechanism; syllabi B2 (break-even ratio)
concepts.mechanism: A loan is repaid from net cash flow, not from net operating income. Reserves and leasing costs come first. DSCR measures the cushion between cash flow and debt service. Break-even occupancy shows how much income can be lost before the loan stops paying. A thin cushion means a small vacancy shock turns a performing loan into a default.

concepts.name: Discounted cash flow, cost of capital and cap rates
concepts.origin: Syllabi B2 (DCF, OCC and r = y + g)
concepts.mechanism: Value is the present value of expected cash flows at an investor's required return. A cap rate is a shortcut: income yield equals required return less expected growth. So a cap rate moves when interest rates, risk premiums or growth expectations move. A lender relying on value must know which assumption would cut value most if it proved wrong.

concepts.name: Financial leverage
concepts.origin: Syllabi B2
concepts.mechanism: Debt raises the equity return when the property yield exceeds the loan constant (positive leverage). It cuts the equity return when the constant is higher (negative leverage). Either way, leverage raises the risk of the equity. A sponsor showing a high levered return may be showing high risk, not skill. Negative leverage also means the property alone cannot cover debt service growth.

concepts.origin: Syllabi B2

concepts.name: Expected loss and credit spreads
concepts.origin: Quality bar 6.1
concepts.mechanism: Expected loss is the average loss a lender should plan for: probability of default × loss given default × exposure at default. It is a cost of doing business, like servicing. The spread over the cost of funds must cover it before any profit. Default also lowers the return actually earned below the promised yield. Early defaults cost more because less interest has been collected (yield degradation). Illustrative only: PD 8%, LGD 35% and exposure $1,000,000 give 0.08 × 0.35 × $1,000,000 = $28,000 of expected loss over the loan's life.

misconceptions.correction: Illustrative (syllabi D1-D2): a 9% three-year loan that defaults in year 3 with 65% recovery earns −6.69%. Add an 8% chance of that default. The probability-weighted average of yields is 9.00% − 0.08 × 15.69 = 7.74%; that is an approximation. The IRR of the expected cash flows (9, 9, then 0.92 × 109 + 0.08 × 65 = 105.48, on 100) is 7.91%, the measure Geltner uses. The gap is 0.17 points.

misconceptions.misconception: Expected loss is what the lender will lose.
misconceptions.correction: It is an average. Actual losses come in clusters during downturns (TM-01), which is why capital is held beyond expected loss.

concepts.name: Risk-based pricing
concepts.origin: Task: risk-based pricing as a concept (owner decision H3)
concepts.mechanism: A loan's spread should pay for five things: spread = cost of funds + expected loss + capital charge + operating cost + margin. Cost of funds is what the lender pays its warehouse or investors. Expected loss rises with the risk rating. The capital charge pays for equity held against losses worse than expected. Operating cost covers origination and servicing. The margin is profit. If a riskier loan is priced like a safer one, the riskier loans win the business and the book's quality falls (TM-05).

concepts.name: Capital stack and subordination
concepts.origin: Quality bar 6.1
concepts.mechanism: Claims on a property are paid in order: senior debt, then mezzanine debt, then preferred equity, then common equity. Losses run the other way. Contractual subordination is a promise in a document. Structural subordination comes from where the claim sits: mezzanine lends to the owner of the borrower, not on the property. Every dollar of junior capital is a buffer for the senior lender. Combined leverage, not senior LTV alone, shows how thin the total equity cushion is. Illustrative (syllabi D12): value falls to $8,000,000, and 6% sale costs leave $7,520,000. That covers senior $6,000,000 and mezz $1,500,000 with $20,000 left, so preferred equity takes the next loss.

misconceptions.correction: Preferred equity often has redemption rights and control triggers. It can act like debt in a downturn.

concepts.name: Refinance and extension risk
concepts.origin: Quality bar 6.1
concepts.mechanism: A bridge loan is repaid by a new loan or a sale, not by its own cash flow. At maturity the take-out lender sizes on its own rules and today's rates. If rates rose or income fell, the take-out is smaller than the payoff. An extension buys time but adds cost and can extend into a deeper loss. So the lender solves for the break-even income and take-out rate on day one, and knows how much room it has.

concepts.name: Interest during construction
concepts.origin: Task: construction risk (interest during construction); syllabi B2
concepts.mechanism: Each draw starts accruing interest on its draw date, so the balance and the interest grow together. Before completion there is no income to pay it. The interest reserve inside the loan pays it, which makes financing cost part of project cost. An average-balance factor estimates the reserve; a draw schedule computes it. A back-loaded or delayed schedule can make the estimate wrong in either direction. Illustrative (syllabi D10): draws of $400,000, $600,000, $900,000 and $1,100,000 at 9% compound to $47,537.80 of interest; a 60% average-balance estimate gives $54,000.00.

concepts.name: Completion and cost-overrun risk
concepts.origin: Task: construction risk (completion and cost overrun)
concepts.mechanism: An unfinished building is worth far less than its cost. So the lender's first risk is that the project stops. Equity first, a contingency line, a completion guaranty, bonds and an in-balance test each move overrun risk away from the lender.

concepts.name: Intercreditor terms and mezzanine foreclosure
concepts.origin: Quality bar 6.1
concepts.mechanism: When a senior and a mezzanine lender share one project, an intercreditor agreement sets who may act and when. Typical terms give the mezz lender notice, cure rights and a purchase option, and limit what the senior may change. A mezz lender holds a pledge of the borrower's ownership interests. It forecloses by a UCC sale of those interests, not by a mortgage foreclosure. The sale must be commercially reasonable in every aspect [VERIFY: UCC 9-610(b), Cornell LII; checked 22 Nov 2026]. It can be fast, which changes who the senior lender's borrower is.

concepts.name: Loss severity and recovery timing
concepts.origin: Quality bar 6.1
concepts.mechanism: Loss given default is the balance plus unpaid interest and costs, less net recovery, as a share of the balance. Time drives it. Every month to recovery adds unpaid interest, taxes, insurance and legal cost. The property state's foreclosure process sets much of that time, so the same loan loses more in a slow judicial state. Early default also hurts yield more, because less interest has been collected (TM-19).

concepts.name: Conditions precedent and the point of no return
concepts.origin: Added so C11 has a home concept
concepts.mechanism: Before funding, the lender can still say no. After the wire, its only protections are the documents and the collateral. Conditions precedent are the last chance to make every earlier approval true on the funding day. A wire is close to irreversible, so a diverted wire is a total loss of the advance. That is why controls sit before release, not after.

concepts.name: Covenants, monitoring and early warning
concepts.origin: Added so C12 has a home concept
concepts.mechanism: Covenants are tripwires set at origination. They let the lender act while the borrower still has options and the property still has value. Reporting, cash-management triggers and sweeps turn a slow decline into an early, contractual response. A lender that waits for a missed payment has usually waited too long.

concepts.name: Workout economics
concepts.origin: Added so C13 has a home concept (loss severity moved to C10)
concepts.mechanism: After default, the lender chooses the path with the lowest net loss, counting time, carry and income collected. Foreclosure is not always best: it is slow, costly and leaves the lender owning the property. A modification can lose less if the borrower adds equity or a guarantor reaffirms. Regulators accept prudent workouts with creditworthy borrowers [VERIFY: OCC Bulletin 2023-23; checked 22 Nov 2026 per needs analysis S6]. That frees the lender to choose on economics.

concepts.name: Loan valuation at a market yield
concepts.origin: Syllabi B2
concepts.mechanism: A loan's price is the present value of its remaining payments at today's market yield. If market yields rise above the note rate, the loan sells below par. That is why a lender holding fixed-rate loans in a rising-rate market cannot sell them without a loss. Illustrative (syllabi D15): $2,000,000 interest-only at 8% with 36 months left, priced at a 9% yield (monthly), is worth $1,947,588.66.
reading: Geltner, Miller, van de Minne, Eichholtz, Lindenthal and Shen, *Commercial Real Estate Analysis for Investment, Finance, and Development*, 4th ed. (Routledge, 2026), Ch. 20

misconceptions.misconception: A performing loan is always worth par.
misconceptions.correction: Price depends on market yield. A sound loan can sell at a discount.

misconceptions.misconception: Only credit problems create loan-sale losses.
misconceptions.correction: Rate moves alone can, as the D15 example shows.

concepts.name: Lifetime expected loss and the allowance
concepts.origin: Syllabi B2 (hazard functions); needs analysis K4
concepts.mechanism: Under CECL, a lender reserves for expected losses over a loan's whole life, not only losses already incurred [VERIFY: FDIC CECL page (ASC 326); checked 22 Nov 2026 per needs analysis S7]. Lifetime loss builds from yearly default chances (hazard rates) applied to the loans that survive each year. Illustrative (syllabi D3): hazards of 1.0%, 1.5% and 2.0% give 1 − (0.99 × 0.985 × 0.98) = 4.44% cumulative default, not 4.50%. Ratings, accrual and charge-offs on single loans roll up into this portfolio estimate.
reading: Geltner, Miller, van de Minne, Eichholtz, Lindenthal and Shen, *Commercial Real Estate Analysis for Investment, Finance, and Development*, 4th ed. (Routledge, 2026), Ch. 21 (hazard functions)

misconceptions.misconception: Add the yearly default rates to get lifetime default.
misconceptions.correction: Loans that already defaulted cannot default again. Multiply survival rates: 4.44%, not 4.50% (illustrative).

misconceptions.misconception: The allowance equals this year's charge-offs.
misconceptions.correction: It is a forward estimate over the remaining life of the book.

concepts.name: Bankruptcy and bankruptcy-remote borrowers
concepts.origin: Professor review 2 (C13 O5 had no theory home)
concepts.mechanism: A bankruptcy filing stops foreclosure at once through the automatic stay [VERIFY: 11 U.S.C. 362(a); Cornell LII; not opened 22 Nov 2026]. Time is the lender's main loss in a stay: interest, taxes and carry run while the collateral cannot be sold. For a single-asset real estate debtor, the court must lift the stay unless the debtor acts within about 90 days. It must file a plan with a reasonable chance of confirmation, or start monthly interest payments [VERIFY: 11 U.S.C. 362(d)(3); Cornell LII; checked 22 Nov 2026] [VERIFY: 11 U.S.C. 101(51B), single asset real estate; Cornell LII; not opened 22 Nov 2026]. So lenders lend to single-purpose entities with separateness covenants. They add recourse that springs to the guarantor on a voluntary filing. That makes a filing costly for the sponsor, not impossible.

misconceptions.misconception: A single-purpose entity cannot file for bankruptcy.
misconceptions.correction: It can. Separateness covenants and springing recourse make a filing less likely and more costly for the sponsor. They do not remove the right to file.

misconceptions.misconception: Once a sale notice goes out, the sale goes ahead whatever the borrower does.
misconceptions.correction: A filing before the sale stops it. The lender must ask the court for relief, and carry costs run meanwhile.
